title: Scaling reads
subtitle: Most apps read far more than they write. Learn the order of steps that serves many more reads without breaking what users see.

c.v: This is a real case, from a paper Facebook published in 2013. Facebook's users read an
more content than they create. So the work was mostly reads, and Facebook put a large
, memcache, in front of MySQL and other data stores.

Loading one popular page fetched an average of 521 different items from that cache. Facebook ran hundreds of cache servers in one cluster. Every web server talked to every cache server, and that caused two problems. Replies that arrived all at once could overload the network switches. And one busy cache server could slow down many web servers.

Simply buying more servers did not fix everything. The paper says popular items only become more popular as you add web servers. It also notes that a single key can be 20% of one cache server's requests.

Then Facebook added data centres in other regions. One master region kept the other regions up to date. Those regions read from local copies of the database, which can lag behind. When lag was large, a user's next page could be missing the change they had just made.
There was no single outage. The read path worked at one size and needed new fixes at the next.

A read path is the route a read takes, from the user's phone to the data. Scaling reads means answering each read as close to the user and as cheaply as you can. Keep the primary database for work only it can do.
. Climb one step at a time, only when your numbers say so. Each step adds a new way for data to be stale.
Every read you answer higher up is a read your database never sees. But every copy of data can be out of date. Choose, for each kind of read, how stale it may be.
First, count reads and writes per second, and find the queries that use the most total time. In PostgreSQL, the
module, once enabled, tracks planning and execution statistics for every SQL statement. These include how often each one ran and its total time.
Facebook's numbers made the choice clear. In a sample of 6.5 million requests to TAO, its graph store, 99.8% were reads and 0.2% were writes.

Send reads to copies of the database, and writes to the primary. This adds read capacity, but replicas lag. TAO measured the lag of its replica databases in other regions. It was under 1 second 85% of the time, under 3 seconds 99% of the time, and under 10 seconds 99.8% of the time.
So plan for seconds, not zero. The
: "I saved it, and it is gone." Facebook's fix was a "remote marker". When a web server in a non-master region writes, it first sets a marker for that key. On a

TAO has a similar idea: a read can be marked "critical" and sent to the master region. The paper's example is a login check, so old credentials are not used.
Our advice: most reads go to replicas. A user's own data, just after they write it, goes to the primary.

PostgreSQL can store the result of a query in a table-like form. Reads are often much faster than querying the base tables. The cost: the data is not always current.

Step 5: read models fed by change data capture
When one database cannot serve every kind of read, build separate
: one model for updates and a different model for reads, maybe in a different database.
In this lesson, a feed table, a search index and a cache can all count as read models.

Facebook copies a small, very busy set of keys to several servers in a pool. Its example: one server holds 100 keys and answers 500,000 requests a second. Each request needs all 100 keys, and 1 million requests arrive each second. Split the keys over two servers, and each server still gets 1 million requests. Copy all keys to both, and each gets 500,000. The cost: every delete must reach every copy.
Other ways to spread a hot key, from our experience:
Cache it inside each app server for a few seconds.
Collapse many misses for one key into one database read.

c.v: Start with numbers: reads per second, writes per second, and the top ten queries by total time.
For each kind of read, ask:
. A bank balance and a like count get different answers.
Decide who reads from the primary. Make it a rule in one place in the code, not a choice in each query.
Watch replica lag and alert on it. Reads that "sometimes show old data" are often lag.
Before a launch or a sale, ask which item everyone will open at once.
"Here is the output of pg_stat_statements for our top 20 queries, and our schema. For each query, say if an index would help, and write the CREATE INDEX statement. Do not suggest caching yet."
"Add read routing to this data layer. Reads go to a replica by default. For 10 seconds after a user writes, that user's reads go to the primary. Show where the 10 seconds is set."
"Design a materialized view for this dashboard query. Add the unique index it needs for REFRESH CONCURRENTLY, and a job that refreshes it every 5 minutes."

q.v: Your database CPU is at 90%. What should you do first?

options.v: Find the top queries by total time, and check their query plans.
Put Redis in front of every table.

why.v: A missing index or a bad query is the cheapest fix. Replicas and caches can come later, if the numbers still need them.

q.v: A user saves their new display name, refreshes, and sees the old one. Reads go to a replica. What is a common fix?

options.v: Read this user's own data from the primary for a short time after they write.
Send all users' reads to the primary forever.

why.v: This is a read-your-writes problem. Only the writer needs the fresh copy, so only their reads go to the primary.

q.v: One cache server is overloaded because of one very popular key. Why does adding more cache servers with the same hashing not help?

options.v: The key still maps to one server, so that server still gets all its reads.
New servers start with no memory.
Hashing does not work with more than ten servers.

why.v: Hashing spreads keys, not reads of one key. Copy the hot key to several servers, or cache it inside each app server.

q.v: What is the main cost of a materialized view?

options.v: Its data is only as fresh as its last refresh.
It slows down every write to the base tables at once.

why.v: PostgreSQL stores the result and updates it only when you refresh it, so reads are fast but can be out of date.

q.v: Facebook's TAO paper reports reads as 99.8% of requests. What does a number like that tell you?

options.v: Caching and read copies will pay off, because almost all the work is reads.
You should shard by write volume first.
You do not need a database.

why.v: Measure the read/write ratio first. When reads are almost all the work, read-side tools give the most benefit.
